sections.h2: Can a squatter take ownership of a Wisconsin house?
sections.html:
Yes, but only after meeting every element of a Wisconsin adverse possession statute for a long, uninterrupted period. The shortest period in the Wisconsin statutes is 7 years. The law sets periods of 20, 10 or 7 years depending on the facts, and the person occupying the land carries the burden of fitting within one of them.

The title holder starts with a legal advantage. Under sec. 893.30, a person who holds legal title is presumed to have been in possession within the time required by law, and another person's occupation is treated as subordinate to that title unless the occupier held the land adversely for 7, 10 or 20 years before the lawsuit. In a Wisconsin house that you own, someone who moved in without your consent has not gained anything by being there a few months.

A tenant is in a different position. Sec. 893.31 says a tenant's possession is the landlord's possession until 10 years after the tenancy ends, or 10 years after the last rent payment if there was no written lease. The adverse possession clocks do not begin to run until that period ends.

sections.h2: How long must someone occupy Wisconsin land to claim it by adverse possession?
sections.html:
The answer is 20 years in the basic case, 10 years with a recorded written instrument, and 7 years when that claim is combined with paying every real estate tax. The table sets out the three statutes.

StatutePeriodMain requirements
Sec. 893.2520 yearsActual continued occupation under claim of title, exclusive of any other right, and only the part actually occupied that is enclosed by a substantial enclosure or usually cultivated or improved
Sec. 893.2610 yearsEntry in good faith under a written instrument or court judgment, recorded with the register of deeds within 30 days of entry, with continued occupation of a material portion of the land described
Sec. 893.277 yearsThe 10-year requirements plus recording within 30 days of execution and payment of all real estate taxes for the 7 years after original entry

Source: Wis. Stat. 893.25 to 893.27, Wisconsin Legislature.

Periods can be added together through predecessors in interest, so a claimant may count time in connection with someone who held the land before. A successful claimant can bring an action under ch. 841 to establish title. A claim also reaches only what was actually occupied under the 20-year rule, and under the 10-year rule it reaches the land described in the instrument, except that possession of one lot in a divided tract is not possession of another lot.

sections.h2: What counts as possession of the land?
sections.html:
The statutes tie possession to actual, continued occupation under a claim of title. Wisconsin lists facts that show possession and occupation under secs. 893.26 and 893.27, and the statute says the list is not limited to these.

  • The land has been usually cultivated or improved.
  • The land has been protected by a substantial enclosure.
  • Although not enclosed, the land has been used for fuel or fencing timber, or for the ordinary use of the occupant.
  • Where a known farm or single lot is partly improved, the part not cleared or enclosed is treated as occupied for the same time as the improved part, following the usual course and custom of the adjoining country.

Good faith is presumed at entry under the written instrument rules unless someone rebuts it. The 20-year rule has no good faith requirement. A person who enters under a deed they know is fraudulent can still start the 20-year period, but not the 10-year period.

Court decisions noted with the statute say that acts consistent with sporadic trespass do not tell an owner that someone is claiming the land. The question is whether the use gave a reasonably diligent owner notice of an ownership claim.

sections.h2: How can a Wisconsin owner stop an adverse possession claim?
sections.html:
An owner can interrupt the clock by recording an affidavit of interruption or by starting a court action or terminating the possession in time. The title holder should act well before the 20, 10 or 7 years end.

Under sec. 893.305, a record title holder can interrupt adverse possession by recording an affidavit of interruption along with a survey certified no more than 5 years before recording, giving notice as the statute requires, and recording proof of that notice. The affidavit gives a legal description, states the owner is the record title holder, describes the possession being interrupted and states that a new period may begin the day after recording. Notice goes by certified mail to a known occupant or neighbor, and by published notice if the person is unknown. When the occupant is a neighbor, the owner must also record a notice of the affidavit on the neighbor's abutting parcel within 90 days after the neighbor receives notice. Recording the affidavit is not an admission that the possession is adverse.

Sec. 893.32 covers entry on the land. A simple entry interrupts adverse possession only if the owner commences an action against the possessor within one year after the entry and before the limitation period runs, or if the entry actually ends the possession and the owner takes possession. The statute says the procedure in sec. 893.305 is not the only way to interrupt a claim.

Governments have their own rule. Under sec. 893.29, no title to land belonging to the state or to a city, village, town, county or school district can be gained by adverse possession.

sections.h2: What can I do about a trespasser or someone living in my Wisconsin property?
sections.html:
Ask the occupant to leave in clear terms, put the notice in writing, and call local law enforcement if the person stays. Wisconsin defines trespass to land in sec. 943.13, and a violation is a Class B forfeiture.

A person commits trespass by entering enclosed, cultivated or undeveloped land of another without the express or implied consent of the owner or occupant. A person also commits it by entering or remaining on land after being told by the owner or occupant not to enter or remain. The notice can be given personally, orally or in writing, or by posting. Posting means a sign at least 11 inches square in at least 2 conspicuous places for every 40 acres, which names the owner or occupant, or markings that read private land together with the owner's name.

If the occupant was ever a tenant, ask the circuit court clerk about the eviction process. When a trespasser leaves belongings in residential rental property, sec. 704.055 requires the landlord to hold the property for 7 days from the date it is discovered. After that the landlord may dispose of it, but must return it promptly if the trespasser asks before disposal. The trespasser, another owner or a secured party can redeem the property before disposal by paying the landlord's expenses.

A lawyer or the circuit court clerk can explain the court process if the occupant refuses to leave. Ask a Wisconsin attorney before you change locks or remove belongings.

sections.h2: How does a possible squatter or title dispute affect selling a Wisconsin house?
sections.html:
An occupant or a claim to part of the land can complicate a sale. Settle who has the right to be in the house first, and keep your records of ownership, tax payments and any notices you sent.

A Wisconsin owner with an occupant who has no right to be there, a boundary dispute or an unrecorded claim can sell to a cash home buyer as-is, once the title company has reviewed the situation. Ask the buyer's title company what it needs before a closing date is set. If the house is vacant, secure it, keep the taxes current and record any deeds right away, since under sec. 706.08 an unrecorded conveyance is void against a later good faith purchaser for value whose conveyance is recorded first.

faqs.q: How many years of occupation does adverse possession need in Wisconsin?
faqs.a: Twenty years under sec. 893.25 in the basic case. The period is 10 years if the claimant entered in good faith under a written instrument or judgment recorded within 30 days, and 7 years if the claimant also paid all real estate taxes for the 7 years after entry.

faqs.q: Do squatters have rights to a Wisconsin house after a few months?
faqs.a: No statute gives a squatter ownership after months. The shortest adverse possession period in Wisconsin is 7 years, and it requires a recorded instrument and payment of all taxes. A person who stays without consent can be a trespasser under sec. 943.13.

faqs.q: Can someone claim land owned by a city or county in Wisconsin?
faqs.a: No. Sec. 893.29 bars adverse possession of land belonging to the state or to a city, village, town, county, school district or other unit of government in Wisconsin. The statute also limits governments from taking private land by adverse possession in most cases.

faqs.q: What should I do with belongings a trespasser leaves behind?
faqs.a: Under sec. 704.055, a landlord of residential rental property must hold the belongings for 7 days from the date they are discovered. After 7 days the landlord may dispose of them, but must return them promptly if the trespasser asks before disposal.

faqs.q: Can a tenant claim my Wisconsin property by adverse possession?
faqs.a: A tenant's possession is treated as the landlord's possession. Under sec. 893.31, the adverse possession periods do not start until 10 years after the tenancy ends, or 10 years after the last rent payment if there was no written lease.
